title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
description: Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh
body: Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.Last year, HMRC estimated, external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise £5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9.The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property. The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits."I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said. Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.In an article for the Renewal journal,, external Haigh argued that raising CGT would "shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy". She said this could be accompanied by measures to ensure that "genuine investment returns are not penalised". Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work".Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to a report in the Financial Times last week, external.Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget.Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living.It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices.The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year. The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers. The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt. In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing.She will tell the prime minister and the chancellor to "live within our means" and signpost her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid. The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks.The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses.

schema.headline: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget

title: Can one photo of your face reveal how ill you are?
description: The 'FaceSurvival' AI tool suggests the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose are the most vital parts of the face to assess when esti
body: The 'FaceSurvival' AI tool suggests the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose are the most vital parts of the face to assess when estimating how long they might have left to live. These metrics applied across many different types of cancers, varying in severity, including ones that had spread to the patient's bones or brain. Most of the cancer patients, who were from the US and the Netherlands, were in their 50s or 60s, but some were children, while others were in their 90s.Doctors already examine patients and run comprehensive checks and tests to judge how unwell they are, and what their prognosis might be. The AI tool, which has a patent application pending, is designed to help doctors doing this work, not replace them. Lead researcher Dr Raymond Mak, from Mass General Brigham in Boston, explained: "As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy."Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment."Mak and colleagues are also evaluating an AI tool for predicting biological age, or how old someone looks, as opposed to their birthday age.The 'FaceAge' tool suggests the skin below the nose and near the mouth - the so-called nasolabial folds and marionette lines - plus the forehead (frown lines), temples (crows' feet) and cheeks are a good indicator of how fast we age. Some lifestyle habits can speed that process up, like heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking.Mak says the tool was "surprisingly consistent" across common real-world photos despite variations in pose, lighting, facial expression and make-up. "It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty [a nose job]," he says. But the researchers stress they need much more data and photos of faces, particularly from lots of different ethnic groups, to determine how well the tools work. They are still very much under development. The research team is inviting the public to take part, external and receive a personalised biological age estimate by uploading their own facial photo the research team. Prof Miroslaw Bober, an expert in video processing and machine learning at the University of Surrey in the UK, says any claims that the tool could track ageing or lifestyle changes over time would be "premature". "This is a promising proof of concept, but it is not ready for clinical use," he said."The tool still needs testing against doctors' own judgement and across different hospitals and patient groups." And he warned: "Predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it."

schema.headline: Can one photo of your face reveal how ill you are?

title: Suspect arrested after Limoges town hall set alight during disorder - French media
description: Figure caption, ByJacob PhillipsUpdated 2 minutes agoA suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hal
body: Figure caption, ByJacob PhillipsUpdated 2 minutes agoA suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.The 40-year-old suspect is known for acts of violence against public officials and has been classified as an "S" subject, meaning he is a potential threat to national security, FranceInfo reported.More than 120 people have already been imprisoned following widespread demonstrations across France, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told CNews-Europe.Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".But French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fireTargeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said.Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday nightEarlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Riots took place across French cities, including the capital ParisMore than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.

schema.headline: Suspect arrested after Limoges town hall set alight during disorder - French media

title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
description: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Vol
body: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause."We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue."This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h). This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step."We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing."I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

schema.headline: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC

title: Champions League: PSG vs Barcelona - Europe's most exciting match-up?
description: Since the start of the 2025 Club World Cup, Barca and PSG rank second and third respectively for most goals scored per match by clubs in Europe's top
body: Since the start of the 2025 Club World Cup, Barca and PSG rank second and third respectively for most goals scored per match by clubs in Europe's top five leagues.Barca have netted 192 times in 68 games at a rate of 2.82 per match, with PSG scoring 154 in 67 games at 2.3 per outing.Only Bayern Munich rank above both.Often dubbed the least competitive of the five major European leagues, PSG have dominated French football in recent times.They have won 12 of the past 14 Ligue 1 titles, including the past five. Three of those five were by nine or more points.Barca are defending La Liga champions and have won three of the past four titles. Last season they finished eight points clear of arch rivals and runners-up Real Madrid.PSG became only the second team in the Champions League era to win it in back-to-back seasons, after Real Madrid.In the past two seasons only Bayern from Europe's big five leagues can match Barca and PSG for back-to-back titles.A further look into recent statistics shows the high praise directed at PSG and Barca is warranted.In expected goals (xG) per league match in Europe's top five leagues since last season, Barca (2.56) and PSG (2.22) rank second and third respectively. Only Bayern (3.06) are above both.Barcelona are also second for goals scored and goals scored per match in that time, with PSG sixth and fifth in those metrics respectively.However, PSG have played fewer league games than Barca, Inter Milan, Real Madrid and Manchester City, who are all high performers in those tables.PSG's squad depth has allowed them to make wholesale changes frequently in Ligue 1 games and still get results.They beat Strasbourg 3-1 on Saturday despite making eight changes to the team that won 4-2 in the Champions League three days earlier."They've earned the right to rest their players," said European football journalist Raphael Honigstein.Barca have also added squad depth this season that has led to an increase in attacking firepower.In 10 of their 11 matches in all competitions this season they have scored three or more goals. In six games they have scored five or more."The biggest and most obvious difference is the squad depth that they've added through some brilliant signings in the likes of Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi," said BBC Sport's Spanish football reporter Elizabeth Conway."They've brought real pace and directness to the attack, and Gabriel Jesus has given them another option up front. It's been pivotal."As well as the collective success of both sides, the individuals starring at PSG and Barcelona are among the world's best.Of the top 14 players on the 2025 Ballon d'Or list, eight of them were current players at PSG or Barcelona.Dembele and team-mate Vitinha finished first and third respectively, with Barcelona teenager Lamine Yamal second.Next Monday's 2026 Ballon d'Or list is also likely to be a similar story. Of the 30 players listed for the award, 13 play for the two clubs.Lamine Yamal, who has eight La Liga goals this season, is among the favourites for this year's award."He's still only 19 and he's still very much developing," said Laurens."The variety that he has in his game, the dribbling and the skills - just everything that he does is just so, so good now."You take him out - [it is] still a very, very good team. Let's say you put Adeyemi on the right and Gordon on the left, and Raphinha - it's still a great front three."But you put Lamine Yamal in there and suddenly it becomes a phenomenal front three."

schema.headline: Champions League: PSG vs Barcelona - Europe's most exciting match-up?

title: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment
description: Job vacancies in the UK have seen their largest fall since the start of the year as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indic
body: Job vacancies in the UK have seen their largest fall since the start of the year as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate.Vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), which said small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring.The ONS figures also showed the unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the lowest for more than a year.The employment rate also rose slightly, and analysts said the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring.The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before Chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget next week.ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment"."The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said."The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor."Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff.The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs.Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms.Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty".However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment".The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added.But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X, external that "businesses can't afford to hire"."This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said.The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the  March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year.Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet"On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment.Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover".But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said.Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened".But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising".The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body.The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates.In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics.

schema.headline: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment

title: Newspaper headlines: 'The French correction' and 'Labour cuts £2bn from Army'
description: Many of the papers focus on the Budget next week. The Times, external says a "tax raid on banks" will be the biggest raiser of revenue, after the Chan
body: Many of the papers focus on the Budget next week. The Times, external says a "tax raid on banks" will be the biggest raiser of revenue, after the Chancellor resisted calls from "allies of Andy Burnham" to increase the rate at which capital gains is charged. According to the Daily Mail, external, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, will warn that the Budget "risks being even worse than the two delivered by Rachel Reeves".The Daily Telegraph, external says "Labour has slashed £2bn from front-line army equipment", dropping plans to develop three new vehicles. The Ministry of Defence said the changes related to "future spend that was uncommitted" and that it was "exploring alternative options".The Sun, external reports that the RAF training jet that crashed in north Wales last month was "flying with its fuel cap off". Officials say the two pilots steered the aircraft away from buildings, and ejected before it exploded on the ground. The paper notes that it's unclear whether the cap's absence "caused or even contributed to the accident." The RAF said it was investigating and wouldn't comment further.The Guardian, external says the prime minister has asked his officials for more "radical options" to "fix" the struggling utility company, Thames Water. The paper reports he previously said he would nationalise the firm, and that one new proposal was to convert outstanding fines into a government stake in the company.The Financial Times, external says the street violence in France has "shocked the public" six months out from a "high-stakes presidential election". Writing in the i Paper, the French writer Agnes Poirier, argues the riots could make a victory for the right wing candidate, Marine Le Pen, more likely. The article says that could make a post-Brexit reset in EU relations "considerably harder", and "leave Britain more isolated in its support for Ukraine".Pictures of a large drone lifting a Ukrainian infantryman appear in some of the papers. The Telegraph, external says it's the first time Ukraine has used an aerial drone to rescue a wounded soldier from the front line. The Mail, external notes the operation was a "last resort", as the man was in a minefield and "could not be safely evacuated by a rescue team or ground vehicle".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'The French correction' and 'Labour cuts £2bn from Army'

title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya
description: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered me
body: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court."All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day."Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.""We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned."My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover."My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said."I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced."I still love him and he is still my pastor."In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder."He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict.

schema.headline: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya

title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
description: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by
body: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.The prime minister announced the changes after concerns were raised that penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished. The new rules include a cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions and for non-payment due to broken ticket machines. Drivers will also get a 10-minute window to leave a car park without facing a penalty.Motoring groups welcomed the changes, but said more needed to be done to stop charges when the driver had done nothing wrong.Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets, but more tickets at private sites are now being issued than ever recorded. According to RAC analysis of government data, some 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025-26, a 17% increase from a year earlier.With each charge worth up to £100, the data suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped."Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat," said Burnham.He added that such charges left "people feeling ripped off and out of pocket".The new rules will give drivers:A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to parkA 10-minute window to leave without facing a penaltyCancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, such as vehicle breakdowns in car parksCancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machinesMaximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups such as forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parkingA freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of PracticeThe new code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales.Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge. The government's Private Parking Code of Practice has been seven years in the making.In 2019, an act of Parliament was passed to create a code but the code was withdrawn in 2022, due to "resistance from the private parking industry", according to the RAC.The current industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024 and updated last year after a review.Angela Rayner, the Communities and Housing Secretary, told BBC Breakfast that parking "shouldn't be a way of making money".Asked if the changes were an admission that motorists have been "ripped off" by parking companies for years, she said: "We're calling time on it. They have regulated themselves and they have their appeals process but we're giving it more meat now."She said the current level of fine was a "proportionate response to when people don't follow the rules".Derek Millard-Smith from the British Parking Association said the group welcomed the changes as it would "increase trust" and said "detterents work" when it came to questions over the cost of fines."We know dog fouling, rail fare dodging, littering - all those levels are around £100 or more because that is a level that is deemed sufficient to change behaviours."

schema.headline: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules

title: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about
description: Image source, Monica ThomasImage caption, Monica is the founder of charity Women's Health Hope ByEmily HoltThis report contains detailed descriptions
body: Image source, Monica ThomasImage caption, Monica is the founder of charity Women's Health Hope ByEmily HoltThis report contains detailed descriptions of medical symptoms.Monica Thomas was in her teens when she started experiencing intimate itching and soreness, but despite numerous trips to the doctors it was dismissed as thrush.Her symptoms got worse, with sores and blisters leaving her in constant pain."I was bed bound for quite a long time because I couldn't walk," she says.Monica says she was examined 28 times in six months before being offered a biopsy.She says "we don't really talk about" gynaecological health as a society so there is a taboo around speaking about symptoms. "Even when we go to the doctors, for me, the embarrassment of having to get undressed...with these doctors looking it is embarrassing," she says."But equally when you're in pain or it's itching and you've got discomfort, living with it is just as bad."The 34-year-old from Suffolk was eventually diagnosed with a condition called lichen sclerosus. Image source, Dr Nighat ArifImage caption, Dr Nighat Arif is author of The Knowledge: Your guide to female health – from menstruation to the menopauseThe lifelong inflammatory condition affects genitals and can cause white patches to form with itching, soreness, splitting and tears, says Dr Nighat Arif, a GP specialising in women's health.It affects men and women but is more common in women over 50, external. There is also a small risk of vulval cancer., external"It's very sore to have sexual intercourse, to pass urine and it gets mixed up with sexually transmitted diseases but it's not contagious," she tells BBC Radio 5 Live podcast That Time of the Month. Research into the prevalence of vulval lichen sclerosus is limited but analysis by the University of Bristol of people in the West Midlands and Warwickshire estimated it affects about 1% of women. Dr Sophie Rees, who helped conduct the research, tells the BBC: "This is almost certainly an underestimate, as we know that there is often a very long delay to diagnosis, and some people probably go their entire lives undiagnosed."There is unfortunately a lot of shame and embarrassment around seeking help for vulval symptoms, as well as a lack of awareness, even amongst healthcare professionals."She adds: "More research is badly needed into true prevalence."'Lonely, horrific time'Monica says multiple misdiagnoses had a "significant" impact on her mental health."I didn't know how to go on... with having no answer, it was just a horrific,  lonely time."She was given medication for herpes. "I was very upset in an appointment with a dermatologist who got quite angry with me because I was like, 'it's not that'. "Then she said that she wanted me to have blood tests for HIV."Doctors told her she was "too young" to have lichen sclerosus."But sadly, women do have it at all ages, you can have it as a child. So I found that really quite difficult, but I always knew that it wasn't right."That Time of the Month What is lichen sclerosus? Listen now. Monica believes there should be more support for those with lichen sclerosus."Once you have a diagnosis, you're still necessarily not treated in the manner that you should, I don't even get a checkup," she says."I manage it on my own with my steroid cream and hope that I'm doing everything right." According to the NHS website,, external the cause of lichen sclerosus is unknown. It might be caused by the immune system mistakenly attacking and damaging your skin. It is not contagious, caused by an infection or by poor personal hygiene. Rubbing or damage to the skin can trigger the condition or make it worse. Image source, Clare BaumhaeurImage caption, Clare urged anyone with any symptoms to make sure they were examined by a doctorClare Baumhaeur, 53, from Kent first experienced symptoms aged five. "I was itchy and I was sore, and I was always told off, I wasn't obviously aware what was going on." Her symptoms worsened into adulthood with tears, blisters and sores."But you don't see other vulvas, so I had no idea mine wasn't normal. I'd had in that time eight smear tests as well and nothing was ever said."In 2016 Clare experienced a tear which did not heal. "I was 43 that year, having it for 38 years at that point, I just couldn't take it any more." A GP told Clare she had herpes and to go to a sexual health clinic, she says she was "shocked" as she had been married for 25 years.  She was eventually referred for a biopsy and was diagnosed with lichen sclerosus and vulval cancer. 'I'd never heard of it'"I'd never heard of lichen sclerosus and also I had a cancer that I'd ever heard of in a place I'd never heard of. "That was the first time I heard the word vulva, no health professional had mentioned it, so it was a lot to take in at that time."Clare had been in remission from vulval cancer for seven years, when a regular check-up revealed a cancer recurrence and she underwent surgery three years ago.In June another check up found pre-cancerous cells and she had a sixth surgery.Clare believes if she had been diagnosed with lichen sclerosus earlier, her cancer may have been diagnosed before it got to stage three."I had to have radiotherapy twice and that's left me with instant early menopause, lymphoedema and nerve damage."Monica encourages women experiencing any changes to their body to keep a diary."It's really important that we get to know our bodies better, to know what's normal for you in your private parts as well, because actually our vulvas do change."If you are being dismissed, get multiple opinions, just keep going back because you don't have to live without answers."She recommended the Lichen Sclerosus Guide, external which has a diagram and template to help you talk to doctors.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Get in touch.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: Broomfield Hospital's NHS trust prosecuted over children's deaths
description: An NHS trust is being prosecuted over the deaths of two children who had sepsis, the BBC has learned.Two charges relate to Zadie Ajetunmobi, three, wh
body: An NHS trust is being prosecuted over the deaths of two children who had sepsis, the BBC has learned.Two charges relate to Zadie Ajetunmobi, three, who died within hours of being taken to Broomfield Hospital, Essex, with a temperature of 40C (104F) in November 2022.A third regards two-year-old Selina Samarina, who was sent home by a doctor at Broomfield in April 2024, only to die two days later.Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust (MSE), which runs the hospital, said it was "working closely" with investigators. It is due before Chelmsford Magistrates' Court in December.Care and treatment was allegedly "not provided in a safe way" to the girls, court documents revealed.The prosecution is being brought by the Care Quality Commission under the Health and Social Care Act.Zadie died within 10 hours of being taken to Broomfield on 10 November 2022, having suffered a cardiac arrest.A post-mortem examination showed her death arose from complications associated with sepsis, external.She was not given a potentially life-saving dose of intravenous antibiotics for more than seven hours.Selina Samarina was taken to Broomfield with symptoms of fever, a rash and irritability on 7 April 2024.She was discharged by a doctor but died there two days later, after her parents readmitted her.The sepsis protocol was triggered on Selina's initial arrival at hospital, however a coroner previously said a doctor of appropriate seniority was not available until two-and-a-half hours later.Selina, who had Down's syndrome, was sent home by a "very junior doctor" in the meantime, assistant coroner Stephen Simblet KC said during an inquest into her death.Adam Sewell-Jones, group chief executive of MSE, said: "We are working closely with the CQC on its investigation. "As there is an ongoing legal process, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."MSE is expected to enter pleas to the three charges on 3 December.Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? title: Esther Rantzen felt 'deprived of choice' over her own death
description: A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death".The farewell message was released as the 86-y
body: A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death".The farewell message was released as the 86-year-old broadcaster and campaigner's family confirmed she had been laid to rest in an "incredibly beautiful" private funeral last week.The Childline founder, who was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, died at her Bramshaw home in the New Forest, Hampshire, on 30 September.A larger memorial service is expected to take place at a later date.Rantzen's daughter Rebecca Wilcox said the family had been inundated with messages since her death."It's been hugely comforting to know that people around the world felt the same way about her as we did," she said.Dame Esther became a prominent campaigner for assisted dying in her later years, something MPs voted against legalising in September.In her note, she wrote: "It would have transformed the way I died if the law had allowed me to ask for assistance to die when my life had become unbearable."I was extremely lucky because I had the talent, skill and support of my local Oakhaven Hospice. "But I was still deprived of any choice over my own death by the current messy criminal law."She said she had become "too physically frail to take the flight" to an assisted dying clinic in Switzerland.Addressing those who opposed the change in the law, she wrote: "Rest assured I will not come back to haunt you, I have better things to do."She also wrote: "Nobody wants to shorten life, just to shorten death."Arthur Stickland, who has been on the committee at Bramshaw Cricket Club for 60 years, said the That's Life! team played annual matches against the village side for about seven or eight years.He said Dame Esther always came along with the show's presenters and backroom staff, and remembered her as "an ordinary person"."You wouldn't know she was actually here. She just mingled amongst the crowd," he said.He said she was a vice president of the club, and that in the village "everybody knew who she was and nobody tried to bother her".Dame Esther presented That's Life! for 21 years and set up Childline in 1986, and later The Silver Line helpline for older people.Her family has asked for donations in lieu of flowers to Oakhaven Hospice, Childline, The Silver Line and Cats Protection.

title: England rugby league: Brian McDermott names unchanged team for World Cup match against France
description: England coach Brian McDermott has named an unchanged 19-man squad for Saturday's Rugby League World Cup match against France.This is despite a 30-12 d
body: England coach Brian McDermott has named an unchanged 19-man squad for Saturday's Rugby League World Cup match against France.This is despite a 30-12 defeat by Tonga in their opening game which has put England's chances of progression to the semi-finals in danger.AJ Brimson retains his place at full-back in the XIII with Jack Welsby among the interchanges.McDermott has kept faith in his players as they prepare for Saturday's Group B-C match in Perth (kick-off 07.35 BST).England men: AJ Brimson, Dom Young, Hugo Savala, Herbie Farnworth, Zach Eckersley, George Williams, Harry Smith, Max King, Brad O'Neill, Luke Thompson, Junior Nsemba, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley.Interchange: Jez Litten, Ben Currie, Ethan Havard, Sam Walters, Jack Welsby, Matty Ashton.Reserves: Kallum Watkins, Mikey Lewis, Ben Talty.In contrast to McDermott, England women's coach Stuart Barrow has made a big selection change before their blockbuster meeting with co-hosts Australia on Saturday.Jenna Foubister will start at half-back, replacing Georgia Roche, after a superb year in the Super League where she was named Woman of Steel.The 19-year-old, who scored on her debut in a 62-0 win against Wales in August 2025, will partner Izzy Rowe in the halves.Rowe scored two tries and kicked nine conversions for 26 points as England opened their World Cup campaign with a 70-6 win against Wales last Saturday.She equalled the record for the most points by an individual England player in a Women's World Cup match.There are two other changes to the XIII, as Molly Jones replaces Georgia Wilson in the centres while Liv Wood plays at prop ahead of Mary Coleman.Lucie Sams is named among the interchanges as England take on reigning champions Australia in Perth with kick-off at 10.05 BST - immediately after the men's match.It will be the first time England have played Australia since they suffered their record defeat - 90-4 - in Las Vegas in March 2025.England women: Fran Goldthorpe, Anna Davies, Molly Jones, Connie Boyd, Amelia Brown, Izzy Rowe, Jenna Foubister, Liv Wood, Keara Bennett, Hollie-Mae Dodd, Jasmin Strange, Eva Hunter, Megan Williams.Interchange: Jodie Cunningham, Vicky Whitfield, Georgia Roche, Lucie Sams.Reserves: Mary Coleman, Georgia Wilson, Lucy Murray.Wales face Samoa in their second ever World Cup match on Friday at 07:45 BST, and coach Thomas Brindle has made several changes.Amberley Ruck replaces Ffion Lewis, with Zoe Heeley moving from centre to the wing.Jade Mullen comes into the centres, while wing Sian Williams also gets a start.Wales women: Leanne Burnell, Zoe Heeley, Jade Mullen, Hannah Bluck, Sian Williams, Amberley Ruck, Tayla Preston, Agnes Wood, Jasmine Gibbons, Emily Hughes, Georgia Cussons, Paige Travis, Bethan Dainton.Interchange: Carys Marsh, Kathryn Salter, Erin Williams, Gracie Hobbs.Reserves: Ffion Lewis, Lucia Davies, Frances Layton, Katie Carr.

title: Criminals in hospital set to lose benefits under new rules
description: Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victi
body: Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.Regulations due to be laid out in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to £800 a month in universal credit over several years.Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, who was stabbed to death by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham, before the killer was sentenced to a hospital order, said she would now "demand" ministers reallocate the funds, which she said was a "no-brainer".The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds a year.The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to parliamentary approval.Currently, serious criminals on hospital orders - where their bed and board is funded by the NHS - continue to receive any benefits they were paid on the outside. Students Barnaby and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital.The parents of Barnaby and Grace met Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden to discuss the change on Monday. Emma Webber said the move was "long overdue". Webber told the BBC it was "not an insignificant amount of money - but it is not just the money"."These criminal patients, who have devastated lives as well as taken lives, [are] not only having their full bed and board and all of their care and rehabilitation provided for them, but also amassing a small fortune while they're inside," she said."The rest of us on the outside are desperately trying to survive and find a way forward in our lives."Webber said she believed the funds should be directed to the victims of serious crime so families "are given the support and the advocacy they need".She added when her son was killed, her family was allocated a support worker who had 50 other families to look after.Webber said: "I beg and I plead, and - actually, I demand - ministers now consider the appropriate reuse of those funds."Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness."Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount."On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits."On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated."The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise."For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price."That ends today, because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it."Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner paid tribute to the families who had campaigned on the matter.She added: "I'm aware the secretary of state has met with the families regarding this and was quite frankly astonished that the situation was as it was, and that these people were receiving benefits."That's why the secretary of state has taken this action and I welcome it."She added the reallocation of funds was "something for the chancellor and secretary of state".Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed."Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control."The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it."The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983, and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.Murder is not included, because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence.The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impact of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.

schema.headline: Criminals in hospital set to lose benefits under new rules

title: 'Give us lessons on personal finance and how to get a job,' teens say
description: We asked teens what schools should teach them about work. This is what they saidByKate BerryBBC Radio 5 Live and Vanessa ClarkeSenior education report
body: We asked teens what schools should teach them about work. This is what they saidByKate BerryBBC Radio 5 Live and Vanessa ClarkeSenior education reporterMore than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests.The online survey, by Survation,, external asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education.Some called for more support with their communications skills and raised concerns about stress management and personal finances.Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was the government's "mission" to ensure teenagers leave school "confident about their next step and equipped with the skills and experience they need to succeed".In England, the government wants to guarantee two weeks' of work experience for every young person, external during secondary school.It's an opportunity not all teenagers are currently given, the survey for the BBC suggests, with more than half of respondents saying they had not done any.When teenagers were asked in the survey what skills or guidance they would like more of at school, the most common responses were more work experience opportunities (44%) and help managing finances (43%).Respondents said they also wanted guidance on how to apply for jobs (42%) as well as how to manage stress and mental health (39%) and develop their communication skills (38%).As part of the Teen Summit project by Radio 5 Live and Bitesize, the BBC followed four students from Newcastle - Param, McKenzie, Jasmine and Javaris - as they tried out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements."I'm terrified about the future. I feel very uncertain about it," 15-year-old Jasmine said.Image caption, Jasmine said she was determined to make the right choices with what she does after schoolJasmine said she enjoyed her placement working on logo designs at web design and development agency Readysalted.But she said the placement made her realise she was probably unsuited to an office job."Hats off to all the workers that have to do this every single day," she said.She said it gave her a real taste of working life, but that she was still worried about making "the wrong decision" around what to do next. "I think about exams and not getting the right grades, which leads to not getting into the right course and then not getting into university, and it's very stressful," she said. "That's always on my mind."A 15-minute walk up the road from Jasmine's placement, near the centre of Newcastle, her classmate Param had his work experience at social housing group Re:Gen. Param said it showed him there was more to work than simply having the right knowledge and understanding."Social skills are just as important as academic skills," he said, after a day of meeting clients and working with people he had never met before.He also spent time with staff carrying out quality checks on social houses, looking for loose fittings or uneven surfaces. "It's given us a taste of the real world," he said. "It's bringing us out of our comfort zones."As an aspiring pilot, he said schools should not just provide work experience opportunities, but additional teaching on other aspects of adult life outside of work."We need to know about houses, mortgages, selling and tax," he said.Image caption, Param said he enjoyed working with new people, which brought him out of his comfort zoneJavaris, who spent a week's placement at Siemens Energy alongside friend and classmate McKenzie, also said the work experience challenged his social skills in a new setting."I've really never been in a workplace with people I don't know, having to socialise and having to teach me about things I've never learned before," he said.Javaris ultimately wants to become a doctor, but said the week had given him an insight into how different parts of a company are run. McKenzie, who wants to study chemistry or become a firefighter, said he enjoyed speaking with people in different jobs and seeing the differences between "hands-on" roles and office work. Image caption, Javaris and McKenzie were able to learn about how a business is run at Siemens Energy In light of AI and new technologies in the workplace, nearly a third of teenagers responding to the survey (32%) said they thought school was preparing them badly for the future of work - although more than half of teenagers said it was preparing them well. One of the areas young people said they wanted more help with was developing communication skills.The BBC set Javaris and McKenzie a challenge to help develop their own communication skills, and put some of their thoughts directly to one of their work experience company's bosses - Aaron Smith, head of business for GT Service at Siemens Energy.So, beyond academic results, what skills are employers really looking for?"You know, you can be extremely academically strong, but if you can't do a presentation, if you can't speak in public, if you are in a group exercise and you step back, these are the kind of softer skills that will be picked out in an apprenticeship assessment centre," Smith said.Figure caption, Teens ask bosses what they're really looking forThe pair were also keen to know if they should be studying AI as part of their education.McKenzie said he thinks AI should be added to the national curriculum, adding that "it's getting harder and harder to see what's AI and what's not".He said he was also concerned about the impact AI may have on the availability of jobs, but added that he was "positive" about his future prospects."Certainly AI is huge within the industry," Smith said."We're actively encouraging AI training, AI learning, AI applications in our business to make us better."'Work experience should be mandatory'The teens' deputy principal, Nigel Holmes, said while it was "really important" for schools to prepare students for their academic qualifications, "we'd be really remiss if we didn't look at those wider employability skills that I think we know are really important".On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted the government to "invest in the success of our young people", with plans for thousands of job opportunities expected this week.Despite the backdrop of AI and a tough jobs market, more than three quarters of teens surveyed said they still felt positive about their futures.In the weeks since their work experience placements, all four students have said they feel clearer about their future opportunities.Javaris said he thinks work experience should be mandatory, and that it "really gives you an insight of what to expect [as] you get older".For Jasmine, who prior to her placement was worried about what the future might hold, things now feel a little less uncertain.After talking to her school careers adviser, she is considering studying psychology."I was kind of worried that I wouldn't get the grades I wanted. I still am a bit," she said."But I definitely know now that even if you don't get grade nines, you'll still have a future and you can still be happy with your job."Listen to more from Teen Summit on BBC Radio 5 Live from 0900Get in touchAre you a young person or parent with thoughts on this? Get in touch.

schema.headline: 'Give us lessons on personal finance and how to get a job,' teens say
